newsitem.title: ITALY: Bank of Italy warns budget may miss EMU targets.
newsitem.headline: Bank of Italy warns budget may miss EMU targets.

text.p: Bank of Italy governor Antonio Fazio gave a cautious welcome on Thursday to the government's 1997 budget but warned it might not be enough to meet tough criteria for founder members of the planned European single currency.
Fazio also said the austerity budget, designed to slash 62.5 trillion lire ($41 billion) off next year's deficit, could have a negative impact on already sluggish economic growth.
Treasury Minister Carlo Azeglio Ciampi said earlier that the budget would win Italy a ticket to the launch of European economic and monetary union (EMU) from its scheduled start in 1999.
Fazio, questioned by a parliamentary budget commission on whether the Treasury sums added up, said the budget was an important move towards balancing the state's heavily-indebted accounts.
"Even if the objectives laid out in the Maastricht Treaty are not reached, the move is nonetheless positive," he said. "We are moving in the right direction."
Fazio said that if the budget package was fully implemented, there might be a more rapid decline in interest rates than had previously been expected.
On the flip side, he warned that the package, which includes a once-off "Euro Tax" to boost state finances, would depress the economy.
The government has forecast economic growth of two percent next year, but Fazio said this would be a best case scenario. "It is highly likely that it will be less than that," he said.
Much of the budget, particularly on the revenue side, has yet to be fully outlined. But Fazio predicted that it would reduce disposable income by some three percent in the private sector next year.
On the spending side, he welcomed government plans to cut state expenditure by 20 trillion lire in 1997. "This represents an important step forward in the elimination of waste." he said.
On the 1996 accounts, Fazio forecast that the state deficit could hit 133 trillion lire against latest official forecasts of overspending totalling 123 trillion lire.
This would push the closely watched ratio between Italy's state sector deficit and gross domestic product (GDP) to around seven percent this year, he said.
The government has said it will cut the ratio to 3.1 percent in 1997, just 0.1 percentage point short of the level demanded by the Maastricht Treaty.
But Fazio pointed out that the whole 1997 budget package, if entirely successful, would cut the deficit figure by just over three percentage points. "Do your own sums," he said.
Asked about the condition of the lira, which has rallied strongly in recent weeks, Fazio said: "The exchange rate is not especially out of kilter."
Prime Minister Romano Prodi called last week for talks to start as soon as possible to fix a level for the lira's re-entry to the European exchange rate mechanism (ERM).
He is eager to return the lira, which crashed out of the ERM in 1992, to the currency grid by the end of the year. $1 = 1,520
